summary:
LunaNav is an interactive platform for exploring and comparing six candidate landing sites near the Moon’s south pole. It brings together terrain, sunlight, darkness, and Earth-visibility data to show how each location could affect a lunar mission.
Users can explore the sites on a 3D Moon, view 360° terrain horizons, test mission dates and observation heights, compare scenarios, and rank sites against mission requirements. LunaNav turns lunar data into a clearer way to ask: which landing site best fits the mission?
LunaNav is a prototype for exploration and early-stage comparison. Its modeled visibility estimates and terrain results are not a substitute for independently validated, mission-grade engineering analysis.
details:
Core platform capabilities

·        Interactive 3D Moon: Explore lunar geography, view the six selected south-polar candidate sites, and navigate between their locations.

·        Mission Planner: Select a landing site, date, and mission parameters to examine modeled solar illumination, darkness duration, and Earth visibility over time.

·        Site Comparison: Compare two landing scenarios side by side using time-series views and common mission-performance indicators.

·        Reverse-KPI Site Optimization: Specify requirements such as minimum continuous sunlight, maximum darkness, and communication constraints. LunaNav checks the six candidate sites against those requirements and ranks suitable alternatives.

·        360° Terrain Horizon Visualization: Inspect modeled horizon profiles around a candidate site to understand how nearby terrain may obstruct the Sun or Earth.

·        Mast Height Analysis: Explore how observation height (0 m, 2 m, or 5 m) changes modeled solar and Earth visibility.

Algorithms and scientific approach

LunaNav uses deterministic, data-driven methods rather than machine learning:

·        Time-Series Analysis: Processes hourly solar and Earth-position observations to estimate sunlight availability, uninterrupted darkness, and potential communication windows.

·        Terrain-Based Visibility Evaluation: Compares the Sun’s and Earth’s elevation angles with modeled lunar terrain-horizon angles to estimate whether either body is obstructed.

·        Rule-Based Comparative Analysis: Evaluates two selected mission scenarios against shared performance indicators to show where their conditions differ.

·        Constraint-Based Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA): Filters candidate sites against user-defined mission constraints, then applies a Weighted Sum Model (WSM) to rank alternatives using sunlight availability (40%), darkness avoidance (30%), and Earth communication availability (30%).
